body:
Why account protection matters

Digital services frequently contain information that should not be accessible to every user. A government employee may need to examine assigned records, while an administrator may require additional permissions to maintain the system.

Protecting these services requires a distinction between verifying a user's identity and deciding what that user is permitted to do.

Authentication: verifying identity

Authentication

Authentication is the process of verifying the identity of a user, device or system before allowing access to protected resources.

When a person enters valid login credentials, the system uses them to establish confidence that the person is associated with the claimed account.

Common authentication methods include passwords, PINs, one-time passwords, authentication applications and biometric verification.

Authentication factors

Authentication methods are commonly grouped into 3 categories.

  • Something you know: A password or PIN.
  • Something you have: A registered authentication device or security token.
  • Something you are: A biometric characteristic, such as a fingerprint.

Multi-factor authentication

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) uses 2 or more different categories of authentication factors to provide additional assurance during login.

For example, a service may require a password and confirmation through a registered authentication device. The password is knowledge-based, while control of the registered device provides a possession-based factor.

Using 2 passwords alone does not provide multi-factor authentication because both belong to the same category: something the user knows.

MFA can make unauthorised access more difficult even if a password is compromised. However, users can still be deceived into disclosing OTPs or approving fraudulent authentication requests. MFA therefore complements rather than replaces safe behaviour.

Authorization and access control

Authorization

Authorization determines what an authenticated or otherwise identified user, program or device is permitted to access or perform.

Access control is the system of rules and safeguards that permits or denies access to particular resources or actions.

Authentication establishes who is requesting access. Authorization determines whether that requester has permission for the requested activity.

Example: a government records system

Consider a digital system used by a district administration.

  • A clerk signs in using authorised login credentials. This is authentication.
  • The system permits the clerk to view records relevant to assigned duties. This is authorization.
  • The system blocks the clerk from changing system-wide administrative settings. This is an example of access control.

Principle of least privilege

The principle of least privilege means that users and processes should receive only the access necessary to perform their assigned tasks.

For example, an employee responsible for viewing application status may not need permission to modify all applicant records.

Restricting unnecessary permissions reduces the potential damage caused by mistakes, compromised accounts or misuse of access.

Public institutions can apply this principle by defining responsibilities, issuing individual accounts, limiting administrative permissions and reviewing access when duties change.

Authentication does not guarantee complete security

An authenticated person may still perform an unauthorised action if permissions are incorrectly assigned. Similarly, a user with valid permissions may be deceived into sharing information with a fraudster.

Therefore, authentication, authorization, access control, software protection and user awareness serve different but complementary purposes.

Prelims focus

  • Authentication verifies a claimed identity.
  • Authorization determines permitted actions or access.
  • Access control enforces permissions and restrictions.
  • MFA uses 2 or more different categories of authentication factors.
  • Least privilege limits access to what is necessary for assigned work.
  • Trap: Successful authentication does not mean a user should have unrestricted access to every record.

[Sources: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, entries Authentication, Authorization and Access Control, including definitions from FIPS 200 and NIST Special Publication 800-162; NIST, Small Business Cybersecurity Glossary, entry Multi-factor Authentication, updated 9 April 2025; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2025-0019, section Strengthen Authentication and Access Control, issued 10 May 2025; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Verifying identity and granting permission are separate security decisions.

title: Authentication and Access Control: Protecting Accounts and Information

body:
What is cyber hygiene?

Cyber hygiene means the routine practices that help keep digital devices, accounts and information secure. Just as regular maintenance reduces the risk of equipment failure, consistent digital safety practices reduce exposure to many common cyber threats.

Cyber hygiene is relevant to individual citizens as well as employees of banks, schools, hospitals, government offices and other organisations.

Basic cyber hygiene for citizens

  • Use strong, unique passwords: Avoid reusing the same password across important accounts. A compromise of 1 service should not automatically expose other accounts.
  • Enable MFA: Use additional authentication factors where supported, especially for important financial and email accounts.
  • Update software: Install genuine updates for devices, browsers and applications to reduce exposure to known weaknesses.
  • Use trusted applications: Avoid installing unknown software sent by strangers or unverified sources.
  • Verify communications: Check unexpected requests independently rather than trusting a message, caller name or search result.
  • Protect financial credentials: Never disclose banking passwords, PINs or OTPs in response to unsolicited requests.
  • Maintain recoverable backups: Keep important files copied to a separate, appropriately protected location.
  • Monitor accounts: Review banking alerts and activity for unfamiliar transactions or access.

Basic cyber hygiene in public institutions

Government institutions require both individual responsibility and organisation-level safeguards. Employees should use their assigned accounts, protect credentials and report suspicious activity. Responsible administrators should maintain supported systems, manage permissions, oversee backups and coordinate responses to incidents.

For example, a public office storing certificates and beneficiary records may use access restrictions to limit who can edit records, security updates to reduce software weaknesses, firewalls to restrict network connections and backups to support recovery.

Matching a threat with the most relevant control

The purpose of a control should guide its selection. A protection that is useful against 1 threat may provide only limited protection against another.

Threat or problemRelevant protectionWhy it helps
Suspicious application containing malwareTrusted software sources and anti-malware protectionReduces exposure to malicious programs and helps detect them.
Known software security weaknessSecurity patch or software updateCorrects the affected weakness.
Unnecessary network connectionFirewallRestricts network traffic under defined rules.
Stolen account passwordUnique password and MFAReduces the likelihood that a stolen password alone permits access.
Employee attempting an unassigned actionAuthorization and access controlRestricts actions according to assigned permissions.
Phishing message requesting an OTPIndependent verification and refusal to disclose the OTPPrevents the user from complying with the fraudulent request.
Ransomware making working files inaccessibleUnaffected, recoverable backupSupports recovery of information after the incident.
Fraudulent UPI payment requestVerification of request, payee and amountReduces the chance of authorising an unintended payment.

Why multiple layers are necessary

Cybersecurity measures are more effective when they complement one another. A device may be updated yet still receive a fraudulent message. A user may have MFA enabled yet be deceived into approving an unauthorised request. A firewall may restrict connections yet fail to prevent a harmful action performed through an otherwise permitted service.

Consequently, protective measures should address different points at which harm might occur: exposure to threats, access to accounts, permissions within systems and recovery after disruption.

Applying the distinctions in familiar situations

Situation 1: A fraudulent bank message

A citizen receives an unexpected message demanding an OTP to prevent account suspension. The main immediate protection is independent verification and refusal to share authentication information. Installing antivirus software is useful general hygiene but does not directly establish whether the caller is genuine.

Situation 2: Unauthorised access to a government account

A public employee's password becomes known to someone else. A strong authentication process, including MFA where supported, helps reduce unauthorised login risk. Access controls can further limit the operations available to the compromised account.

Situation 3: Files become unavailable after malware infection

A public office cannot access working records after ransomware infection. Prevention involves updates, anti-malware protection and safe practices. Recovery may depend on unaffected backups and assistance from the authorised technical team.

Understand the purpose of each safeguard

Firewalls mainly control network communication. Anti-malware software addresses malicious programs. Updates correct known weaknesses. Authentication verifies identity. Access control restricts permissions. Backups support recovery. Awareness and independent verification help prevent deception-based fraud.

Prelims focus

  • Cyber hygiene includes routine preventive practices by users and institutions.
  • Strong passwords and MFA reduce account-access risks.
  • Least privilege reduces unnecessary permissions.
  • Backups support recovery rather than guaranteeing prevention.
  • Independent verification is central to preventing phishing and impersonation fraud.
  • Trap: No single control provides complete protection against every cyber threat.

[Sources: CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2025-0019, sections Strengthen Authentication and Access Control, Patch Management, Secure Network and Endpoint Devices, Implement Robust Data Protection Strategies and Conduct Employee Awareness and Training, issued 10 May 2025; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2024-0050, Preventing Online Scams, Best Practices and Recommendations, issued 24 October 2024; Reserve Bank of India, Consumer Awareness: Cyber Threats and Frauds, Safe Digital Banking Practices, dated 28 January 2022; NIST, Small Business Cybersecurity Glossary, updated 9 April 2025; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Cybersecurity protection combines prevention, restricted access and recovery.

title: Cyber Hygiene and Matching Threats with Protective Controls

body:
Why institutional roles matter

Cyber threats affect both individuals and public systems. Citizens need reliable methods to report cybercrime, while organisations require technical guidance, incident assistance and coordination with the responsible authorities.

Different institutions perform different functions. A national technical incident-response organisation is not the same as a police agency investigating fraud.

Indian Computer Emergency Response Team

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) operates under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India.

CERT-In performs national computer-security incident-response functions. Its work includes issuing security advisories, providing incident-related guidance, analysing security threats and supporting prevention and recovery.

CERT-In also operates the Cyber Swachhta Kendra, a Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre that promotes awareness and assists users in addressing certain malware infections.

CERT-In is not the ordinary police complaint portal

CERT-In primarily performs technical cybersecurity and incident-response functions. Cybercrime complaints requiring criminal investigation are handled through the appropriate law-enforcement mechanisms.

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) is associated with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

I4C supports coordination among law-enforcement agencies and other stakeholders to address cybercrime. It assists with national efforts relating to cybercrime prevention, reporting, awareness and capacity building.

I4C became an attached office of the Ministry of Home Affairs on 1 July 2024.

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and helpline

The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal provides a government mechanism through which citizens can report cybercrime complaints online.

The portal covers various categories of cybercrime, including online financial fraud, mobile-related offences, social-media offences and other cyber-enabled crimes.

The 1930 national cybercrime helpline is particularly important for promptly reporting online financial fraud.

As of 16 November 2026, the official national reporting arrangements identify the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and helpline 1930 as channels for cybercrime reporting. Complaints submitted through the national system are handled by the relevant law-enforcement agencies or police authorities based on the information supplied.

State Police and Gujarat's role

Cybercrime investigation and related law-enforcement action involve the competent police authorities. In Gujarat, the State Police and its cybercrime units form part of the institutional response to cybercrime.

A citizen in Gujarat who experiences online financial fraud can use the national reporting arrangements and contact the relevant bank or payment provider. Other suspected cybercrimes can be reported through the national portal or appropriate police channels.

Gujarat's CAWACH Kendra

CAWACH Kendra stands for Cybersecurity Awareness And Creative Handholding Kendra. It is an initiative of the Education Department, Government of Gujarat, in collaboration with the Home Department, directed at improving cybersecurity awareness and cyber-safe behaviour among college students.

Its educational role should be distinguished from the investigation of cybercrime by law-enforcement agencies.

Reserve Bank of India

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issues public awareness guidance on safe digital banking and payment-related fraud.

Its advisories warn citizens against disclosure of passwords, OTPs, PINs and other confidential banking information. The RBI's role in public education and financial-sector oversight is different from police investigation of an individual cybercrime complaint.

Institutional roles at a glance

Institution or mechanismAdministrative connectionRelevant function
CERT-InMeitY, Government of IndiaCybersecurity incident response, advisories and technical guidance.
I4CMinistry of Home AffairsNational coordination of efforts against cybercrime.
National Cyber Crime Reporting PortalGovernment of India cybercrime reporting mechanismOnline submission of cybercrime complaints.
1930 helplineNational cybercrime reporting arrangementsPrompt assistance in reporting online financial fraud.
State Police cybercrime unitsRelevant State Police authoritiesLaw-enforcement action and investigation.
RBIIndia's central bankFinancial-sector oversight and digital-banking safety awareness.
CAWACH KendraEducation Department, Government of Gujarat, with Home Department collaborationCybersecurity awareness and education.

Basic response after suspected cybercrime

Appropriate action depends on the nature of the incident.

  1. Recognise suspicious activity: Examples include an unauthorised transaction, unfamiliar account access or a device behaving as though it has been compromised.
  2. Use trusted channels: Contact the affected bank, service provider or responsible institutional security team using independently verified contact details.
  3. Report promptly: For online financial fraud, use the national cybercrime helpline 1930 and the official reporting portal. Other cybercrimes may be reported through the portal or competent police authorities.
  4. Preserve relevant information: Retain transaction references, suspicious messages and other relevant records where available, without unnecessarily altering possible evidence.
  5. Follow authorised protective guidance: Affected public employees should inform their designated IT or cybersecurity team and follow approved procedures.

Prompt reporting improves the opportunity for authorities and financial institutions to act, but it does not guarantee reimbursement or recovery of lost funds.

Overall understanding of threats and controls

Cybersecurity is not limited to installing protective software. Citizens must recognise deceptive communications and protect authentication details. Organisations must maintain secure systems, restrict permissions, preserve recoverable data and coordinate appropriately when incidents occur. Public institutions support these efforts through awareness, technical guidance, complaint reporting and law enforcement.

Prelims focus

  • CERT-In operates under MeitY and performs national cybersecurity incident-response functions.
  • I4C operates under the Ministry of Home Affairs and supports cybercrime coordination.
  • I4C became an attached office of MHA on 1 July 2024.
  • The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal accepts cybercrime complaints online.
  • Helpline 1930 is associated with reporting online financial fraud.
  • Gujarat's CAWACH Kendra focuses on cybersecurity awareness and education.
  • Trap: CERT-In, I4C and the police do not perform identical functions.

[Sources: CERT-In, Roles and Functions, official website; CERT-In, Cyber Swachhta Kendra, Frequently Asked Questions, sections Introduction, Functions and Administration; Ministry of Home Affairs, Cyber and Information Security Division, Overview about I4C, consulted 16 November 2026; Government of India, National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, About the Portal, Frequently Asked Questions and Cybercrime Reporting Services, status consulted 16 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, CAWACH Kendra, official website, Cyber Awareness and About the Initiative, consulted 16 November 2026; Reserve Bank of India, Consumer Awareness: Cyber Threats and Frauds, press release dated 28 January 2022.]
